context_blurb:
Flip a switch and a lamp lights. Behind it lie a few rules of charge flowing round a circuit, and two discoveries by Michael Faraday: a current and a magnet can make motion, and motion and a magnet can make a current.

Current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes with an ammeter; voltage is the push that drives it, in volts; resistance is how hard a material holds back the flow, in ohms. Every bit of charge that flows into a bulb flows out again, so an ammeter reads the same current on both sides of it. The bulb takes energy, given off as light and heat, not charge.

In Cologne the schoolteacher Georg Ohm read the current in test wires from a magnetic needle's turn, with a steady push from a thermocouple of copper and bismuth, one end in ice and one in boiling water. His 1827 book gave Ohm's law: current rises in step with the voltage and falls as resistance rises, and a wire of one metal resists more the longer and less the thicker it is. So at the same push a shorter or thicker wire carries more current and a longer one less, and only a longer wire carrying more current would have broken the law. One Berlin journal's review dismissed the book as "a web of naked fancies"; the doubters mostly objected to treating electricity by mathematics. Gustav Fechner's careful tests of 1831 bore Ohm out.

Parts in series sit end to end on one path and share the battery's voltage; take one out and the path breaks, as on old strings of holiday lights. In parallel, every part has a branch of its own across the source. So when three bulbs share one battery, only if all three are in parallel can any one come out and leave the other two lit.

A house is wired in parallel because each lamp and socket, joined straight across the supply, then gets its full voltage whatever else is on. Old filament bulbs of 60 and 25 watts, the energy each uses each second, get the same voltage from house sockets. With the same push, more current flows only where there is less resistance, so the brighter 60-watt bulb has the filament with less resistance, not more.

In September 1821, at London's Royal Institution, Faraday made the first electromagnetic motor. He fixed a magnet on end in a bowl of mercury, a liquid metal, and let a hanging wire dip into it. When he sent a current down the wire, it swept round and round the magnet for as long as the current ran. The magnet's push on a current is at right angles to both the current and the field, so it shoves the wire sideways, never in; most motors since use that push.

Faraday then sought a current from magnetism; steady currents and still magnets gave nothing. On 29 August 1831 he wrapped two unjoined coils on an iron ring, one on a battery and one on a galvanometer, a needle meter for current. The needle flicked one way as the battery was connected and the other way as it was disconnected, but sat still while the current flowed steadily. Only a changing current in one coil makes a current in the other.

Later that year Faraday thrust a bar magnet into a wire coil joined to a galvanometer; the needle jumped as it entered, but a magnet resting in the coil gave nothing. Pushed in faster, the magnet changes the field through the coil faster, and the faster that field changes, the bigger the current and the flick. Power-station generators work by just such a changing field in coils.

That October Faraday built the first electromagnetic generator, a copper disc spinning between the arms of a horseshoe magnet, its axle and rim wired to a galvanometer. Each part of the turning copper sweeps across the magnet's field, and a conductor moving through a field has a current driven along it, so a current flows for as long as the disc spins. The magnet need not move.

Motor and generator are one machine run two ways: at Vienna in 1873 Hippolyte Fontaine wired an idle Gramme generator to a working one by mistake, and its shaft spun. Coasting downhill, an electric car's turning wheels spin its motor, which now works as a generator, charging the battery and holding the car back. This is regenerative braking.
